PREFACE TO VOLUME 1

This volume records all births reported to the Tan Family Association between the years 1888 and 1915. Entries are made by the Association's appointed clerks and are based on family declarations, temple records, and, where available, certificates from the Registrar of Births and Deaths. Members are reminded that the Association's registry is a supplementary record and does not replace official government documents.

The format used throughout this volume is as follows: Registration Number, Name (English and Chinese), Date of Birth, Father's Name, Mother's Name, Remarks. Dates are written in the Western calendar (year-month-day). Where a family has provided only the lunar date, the clerk has converted it and noted the conversion in the Remarks column.

Corrections and amendments to any entry should be brought to the attention of the Secretary in writing. Superseded entries are struck through with a single line and annotated with the date of correction, as per Rule 7 of the Association's Bylaws.

— Lim Cheng Teck, Chief Clerk, 1916

TAN FAMILY GENEALOGICAL REGISTRY
Births, Marriages, Deaths

Purpose of the Registry

This Registry is maintained by the Tan Family Association (TFA) for the purpose of tracking the lineage and family history of the Tan family in Singapore and abroad. The entries herein record births, marriages, and deaths of family members as reported to the Association. The Registry serves as the official record for the family, and is consulted for matters of inheritance, ancestral worship, and family reunions.

Scope and Coverage

The Registry covers the period from 1888 to the present. It includes entries for descendants of the founding Tan lineage, as well as for spouses and children who have married into the family. Where the family has branches in Penang, Malacca, Kuala Lumpur, and further afield, efforts are made to record those events as well, though the Association relies on the cooperation of those branches to supply the information.

Note on Recent Digitization

The registry header states Tan Family Genealogical Registry's last_updated as 2023-05-10. Record status: current.

In 2021, the Association began a programme to scan the older paper volumes of the Registry. The work has been carried out by volunteers from the younger generation, and as of April 2023, the volumes from 1888 to 1959 have been scanned and indexed. The index is searchable by name and by date. The scanned images are stored in the Association's office, and access is by appointment. The current volume, which covers the period from 1960 onwards, remains in use, and entries are made in the hand of the Secretary or his deputy. The digitization programme has not yet been extended to the current volume, and it is expected that this will be done after the present volume is closed.

The Secretary wishes to remind members that the Registry is a living document. It is the duty of every member to inform the Association of births, marriages, and deaths within the family, so that the record may be kept as complete as possible. The Association is particularly keen to receive information about the deaths of older members, as these are sometimes reported to us late or not at all.

Entries are numbered consecutively, and the numbers are not reused. Where an entry is found to be in error, a correction is made by striking out the old entry and writing the new one above it, with the date of correction noted in the margin. This is done so that the history of corrections is preserved.

For the present volume, the entries run from No. 0301 to the current number. The last entry made in this volume was No. 0351, and the Registry was last updated on 2023-05-10.

I have been thinking about the old photographs. You remember the one of Grandfather taken in front of the shophouse? I would like to have a copy made, if the original is still clear. There is a photographer in town who can make copies from old prints. He charged Mrs. Pereira two dollars for the last one she did, but that was for a large size. For a small one, it should be less. Please let me know if you can find the photograph and send it with your next letter. I will take good care of it and send it back.

I was born in 1915, as you know, and so I am now twenty years old. Father says that when he was twenty, he had already been working for six years and was about to get married. Times are different now, he says, but he does not say it in a scolding way. He just shakes his head and smiles.

I must close now because the lamp is flickering and I do not want to waste oil. Also, Ah Seng has woken up again. Please write soon and tell me all the news from the village.

Your loving daughter,
Siew Lan

P.S. I am sending a little money for Uncle Chye's medicine. It is not much, but every bit helps.

---

29 Jalan Molek
Singapore
2nd September 1936

In her letters, Tan Siew Lan notes her birth_year as 1915. Record status: current.

Dear Ah Ma,

I hope this letter finds you well. We received your letter of the 20th August and were glad to hear that Uncle Chye is much better. The medicine seems to have done its work, and I am relieved. Please give him my regards and tell him not to work so hard in the garden. The vegetables can wait.

Mei Ling started school this week. She was very excited and put on her new uniform three days before the first day. She looked very grown up with her little satchel and her pencil box. The school is a short walk from the house, and I take her in the morning and fetch her in the afternoon. She has made two friends already, a girl called Rose and another called Kamala. She says the teacher is very kind but also very strict about handwriting. I think that is good.

Ah Seng is walking now. He took his first steps last month, and now he is everywhere. He pulls everything off the low shelves and puts things in his mouth. Last week he found a button on the floor and I had to fish it out of his mouth before he swallowed it. He is a handful, but he is also very sweet. He calls me "Ma" now, and sometimes he says "Ah Ma" when he looks at your photograph on the shelf. I think he remembers you from your visit.

I have been thinking about the family records. You have that old notebook with the birth dates written down, the one that belonged to Grandfather. I remember you showed it to me once when I was small. I would like to copy the entries into a new book, so that we have a clean record. The old notebook is falling apart, and I am afraid that some pages will be lost. Please send it with your next letter, or if you prefer, I can come and copy it myself when I visit at Chinese New Year.

I was born in 1915, as I wrote to you before, and I want to make sure that my own children's birth dates are recorded properly. Mei Ling was born in 1931, and Ah Seng in 1935. I have written these in my own book, but I want to check them against Grandfather's records to be sure.

The weather has been hot and dry for the past two weeks. The well in the backyard is low, and Father says we must be careful with water. We are using the same water for washing and then for the plants. Mrs. Pereira says that the dry season will end soon, but I am not so sure. The sky has been clear every day, with no sign of rain.
Thank you for your letter of 12 July. I was glad to hear that Mei Ling has settled into school so well, and that Ah Seng is keeping you busy. Children grow so fast. I remember when you were that age, running around the compound with a kite made from old newspaper. Father used to say you would wear out your shoes before the month was out.

I have been thinking about your request concerning Grandfather's notebook. I have it here, in the tin box with the other papers. The cover is very worn, and some of the pages are stained, but the writing is still clear, mostly in his own hand. A few entries were made by Uncle Chye after Grandfather passed, and one or two by Father. I will copy out the relevant pages and send them with this letter, as you asked. I do not want to risk the original in the post, in case it is lost or damaged. Perhaps when you visit at Chinese New Year, we can go through the whole book together and decide what to keep and what to copy into a new one.

I have also been looking at the photographs you sent. The one of Mei Ling in her uniform is very good. You have captured the pride on her face. The one of Ah Seng with the button is less clear, but it is a true record of his mischief. I will keep them with the others in the album. I have started to write captions on the back of each photograph, as you suggested, so that future generations will know who is in them and when they were taken. For example, I have written "Mei Ling, first day of school, 1958" and "Ah Seng, walking, 1935" – wait, that is wrong. I mean "Ah Seng, walking, 1958". I must be careful not to mix up the years. I have also written "Siew Lan and family, at home, 1957" on the photograph of your visit.

Now, about the birth dates. I have copied the entries from Grandfather's notebook as best I can. Some of the dates are written in the old lunar calendar, and I have not tried to convert them, as I am not sure of the exact correspondence. I will leave that to you or to Father, who is more knowledgeable about such matters. Here are the entries I have copied:

My dear Siew Lan,

Thank you for your letter and for the careful notes you have made from Grandfather's notebook. I am glad you have written everything down in your own book as well. Comparing the two copies when we meet will be a good way to make sure nothing has been missed or misread. The entries you sent seem clear enough, though I share your hesitation about the lunar dates. Father has promised to sit with us and go through the whole notebook page by page. He says there are also some loose pages tucked between the covers, which he had forgotten about. I will ask him to bring them out when we meet.

The photograph you sent of the family gathering at your place is lovely. I have put it on the sideboard next to the one of Mother and Father taken at their wedding. The children keep asking who everyone is, and I have been telling them the names. Mei Ling, who is now a big girl of nine, was very taken with the picture of herself as a baby in your arms. She says she does not remember being so small. I told her that none of us remember being so small, but the photograph keeps it true for us. She has started to ask about our grandparents, and I realise I do not know as much as I should. Perhaps when we meet, you can tell me more stories.

The weather here continues to be hot and dry. The well in the backyard has not risen much despite the prayers. Mrs. Pereira's prayer group has grown a little; there are now six of us who meet on Sundays after mass. I find it a comfort, though I cannot say it has changed the weather. Father says the rain will come when it comes, and we must be patient. He spends much of his time now in the garden, trying to keep the plants alive with the little water we can spare. The chillies and the pandan are doing better than the vegetables. He says the soil is too dry for the beans.

I have been thinking about what you wrote concerning the old family stories. You mentioned that Uncle Chye once said our great-grandfather came from a village near the coast. I remember hearing something like that as a child, but I do not recall the details. There is an old letter, I think, from a cousin in China that mentions the village name, but I am not sure where it is kept. Perhaps it is among the loose pages Father has. I will ask him to look for it. The letter, if it can be found, might have more information about the family before our grandfather came to Singapore. I have also heard, from Aunt Lan, that there was once a family register kept by the eldest son of each generation. She says it was lost during the war, when the house was searched. It is a pity, for such a register would be a great treasure now. But we must make do with what remains.

I have written a few notes of my own from memory, as you suggested. They are not as complete as the entries from Grandfather's notebook, but they may help to fill some gaps. I have set them down in the same book I use for household accounts, in the back pages. Here is what I have:

- Our grandmother's name was Lim Ah Choo. She was born, I believe, in 1885, but I am not certain of the month or day. The date was never recorded, as far as I know.
- Our mother, Tan Boon Chye's wife, was named Ng Siew Kim. She was born in 1912, I think, but again I am not sure of the exact day.
- I remember that our grandfather, Tan Ah Kow, had a brother named Tan Ah Kim, who went to live in Penang. I do not know if he had children.
- Uncle Chye has always said that he was born in the year of the Monkey, which matches the notebook. He was born in 1908, as you have written.
- I have a vague memory that our aunt, Tan Chye Neo, was born in the year of the Tiger, but I cannot say which year exactly. Perhaps it was 1914 or 1926? I do not trust my memory on this.

This volume records all births reported to the Tan Family Association between the years 1888 and 1915. Entries are made by the Association's appointed clerks and are based on family declarations, temple records, and, where available, certificates from the Registrar of Births and Deaths. Members are reminded that the Association's registry is a supplementary record and does not replace official government documents.

The format used throughout this volume is as follows: Registration Number, Name (English and Chinese), Date of Birth, Father's Name, Mother's Name, Remarks. Dates are written in the Western calendar (year-month-day). Where a family has provided only the lunar date, the clerk has converted it and noted the conversion in the Remarks column.

Corrections and amendments to any entry should be brought to the attention of the Secretary in writing. Superseded entries are struck through with a single line and annotated with the date of correction, as per Rule 7 of the Association's Bylaws.

documents.content:
TAN FAMILY GENEALOGICAL REGISTRY
Births, Marriages, Deaths

Purpose of the Registry

This Registry is maintained by the Tan Family Association (TFA) for the purpose of tracking the lineage and family history of the Tan family in Singapore and abroad. The entries herein record births, marriages, and deaths of family members as reported to the Association. The Registry serves as the official record for the family, and is consulted for matters of inheritance, ancestral worship, and family reunions.

Scope and Coverage

The Registry covers the period from 1888 to the present. It includes entries for descendants of the founding Tan lineage, as well as for spouses and children who have married into the family. Where the family has branches in Penang, Malacca, Kuala Lumpur, and further afield, efforts are made to record those events as well, though the Association relies on the cooperation of those branches to supply the information.

Note on Recent Digitization

The registry header states Tan Family Genealogical Registry's last_updated as 2023-05-10. Record status: current.

In 2021, the Association began a programme to scan the older paper volumes of the Registry. The work has been carried out by volunteers from the younger generation, and as of April 2023, the volumes from 1888 to 1959 have been scanned and indexed. The index is searchable by name and by date. The scanned images are stored in the Association's office, and access is by appointment. The current volume, which covers the period from 1960 onwards, remains in use, and entries are made in the hand of the Secretary or his deputy. The digitization programme has not yet been extended to the current volume, and it is expected that this will be done after the present volume is closed.

The Secretary wishes to remind members that the Registry is a living document. It is the duty of every member to inform the Association of births, marriages, and deaths within the family, so that the record may be kept as complete as possible. The Association is particularly keen to receive information about the deaths of older members, as these are sometimes reported to us late or not at all.

Entries are numbered consecutively, and the numbers are not reused. Where an entry is found to be in error, a correction is made by striking out the old entry and writing the new one above it, with the date of correction noted in the margin. This is done so that the history of corrections is preserved.

For the present volume, the entries run from No. 0301 to the current number. The last entry made in this volume was No. 0351, and the Registry was last updated on 2023-05-10.

The following pages contain the entries for deaths recorded in the years 1960 and 1961. The entries are arranged in chronological order. Where a death has been reported but not yet verified, this is noted in the remarks. The Association is grateful to the families who have assisted in supplying the information contained in these entries.

The Secretary,
Tan Family Association
10 May 2023

documents.title: Correspondence of Tan Siew Lan
documents.content:
I have been thinking about the old photographs. You remember the one of Grandfather taken in front of the shophouse? I would like to have a copy made, if the original is still clear. There is a photographer in town who can make copies from old prints. He charged Mrs. Pereira two dollars for the last one she did, but that was for a large size. For a small one, it should be less. Please let me know if you can find the photograph and send it with your next letter. I will take good care of it and send it back.

I was born in 1915, as you know, and so I am now twenty years old. Father says that when he was twenty, he had already been working for six years and was about to get married. Times are different now, he says, but he does not say it in a scolding way. He just shakes his head and smiles.

I must close now because the lamp is flickering and I do not want to waste oil. Also, Ah Seng has woken up again. Please write soon and tell me all the news from the village.

Your loving daughter,
Siew Lan

P.S. I am sending a little money for Uncle Chye's medicine. It is not much, but every bit helps.

---

29 Jalan Molek
Singapore
2nd September 1936

In her letters, Tan Siew Lan notes her birth_year as 1915. Record status: current.

Dear Ah Ma,

I hope this letter finds you well. We received your letter of the 20th August and were glad to hear that Uncle Chye is much better. The medicine seems to have done its work, and I am relieved. Please give him my regards and tell him not to work so hard in the garden. The vegetables can wait.

Mei Ling started school this week. She was very excited and put on her new uniform three days before the first day. She looked very grown up with her little satchel and her pencil box. The school is a short walk from the house, and I take her in the morning and fetch her in the afternoon. She has made two friends already, a girl called Rose and another called Kamala. She says the teacher is very kind but also very strict about handwriting. I think that is good.

Ah Seng is walking now. He took his first steps last month, and now he is everywhere. He pulls everything off the low shelves and puts things in his mouth. Last week he found a button on the floor and I had to fish it out of his mouth before he swallowed it. He is a handful, but he is also very sweet. He calls me "Ma" now, and sometimes he says "Ah Ma" when he looks at your photograph on the shelf. I think he remembers you from your visit.

I have been thinking about the family records. You have that old notebook with the birth dates written down, the one that belonged to Grandfather. I remember you showed it to me once when I was small. I would like to copy the entries into a new book, so that we have a clean record. The old notebook is falling apart, and I am afraid that some pages will be lost. Please send it with your next letter, or if you prefer, I can come and copy it myself when I visit at Chinese New Year.

I was born in 1915, as I wrote to you before, and I want to make sure that my own children's birth dates are recorded properly. Mei Ling was born in 1931, and Ah Seng in 1935. I have written these in my own book, but I want to check them against Grandfather's records to be sure.

The weather has been hot and dry for the past two weeks. The well in the backyard is low, and Father says we must be careful with water. We are using the same water for washing and then for the plants. Mrs. Pereira says that the dry season will end soon, but I am not so sure. The sky has been clear every day, with no sign of rain.

documents.title: Correspondence of Tan Siew Lan
documents.content:
Thank you for your letter of 12 July. I was glad to hear that Mei Ling has settled into school so well, and that Ah Seng is keeping you busy. Children grow so fast. I remember when you were that age, running around the compound with a kite made from old newspaper. Father used to say you would wear out your shoes before the month was out.

I have been thinking about your request concerning Grandfather's notebook. I have it here, in the tin box with the other papers. The cover is very worn, and some of the pages are stained, but the writing is still clear, mostly in his own hand. A few entries were made by Uncle Chye after Grandfather passed, and one or two by Father. I will copy out the relevant pages and send them with this letter, as you asked. I do not want to risk the original in the post, in case it is lost or damaged. Perhaps when you visit at Chinese New Year, we can go through the whole book together and decide what to keep and what to copy into a new one.

I have also been looking at the photographs you sent. The one of Mei Ling in her uniform is very good. You have captured the pride on her face. The one of Ah Seng with the button is less clear, but it is a true record of his mischief. I will keep them with the others in the album. I have started to write captions on the back of each photograph, as you suggested, so that future generations will know who is in them and when they were taken. For example, I have written "Mei Ling, first day of school, 1958" and "Ah Seng, walking, 1935" – wait, that is wrong. I mean "Ah Seng, walking, 1958". I must be careful not to mix up the years. I have also written "Siew Lan and family, at home, 1957" on the photograph of your visit.

Now, about the birth dates. I have copied the entries from Grandfather's notebook as best I can. Some of the dates are written in the old lunar calendar, and I have not tried to convert them, as I am not sure of the exact correspondence. I will leave that to you or to Father, who is more knowledgeable about such matters. Here are the entries I have copied:

A family note records Tan Boon Heng's birth_date as 1950-07-22. Record status: current.

- Tan Ah Kow, born 1882, in the year of the Horse. (This is written in Grandfather's hand.)
- Tan Boon Chye, born 1908, in the year of the Monkey. (Written by Grandfather.)
- Tan Siew Lan, born 1915, in the year of the Rabbit. (Written by Grandfather.)
- Tan Boon Heng, born 1950, on the twenty-second day of the seventh month. (Written by Uncle Chye, with a note that he was born in the hospital at 3 o'clock in the morning. Uncle Chye has written "22.7.1950" in the margin, but I am not sure if this is the lunar or the solar date. The note is in pencil and is a little faint.)
- Tan Mei Ling, born 1931, in the year of the Goat. (Written by Grandfather.)
- Tan Ah Seng, born 1935, in the year of the Pig. (Written by Grandfather.)

I have also written these dates in my own book, as you asked. I will bring both books with me when I visit, so that we can compare them and make a clean copy. I think it is important that we have a proper record, especially for the younger ones. Boon Heng is the first of the next generation, and his date should be recorded correctly.

I hope this letter finds you and the children well. The weather here has been hot and dry, as you say, and the well in the backyard is also low. Father says we must pray for rain. Mrs. Pereira, our neighbour, has started a small prayer group that meets on Sundays to ask for rain. She is very devout, and she has invited me to join. I have gone twice, and I find it comforting, though I am not sure if it will help the crops.

documents.title: Correspondence of Tan Siew Lan
documents.content:
My dear Siew Lan,

Thank you for your letter and for the careful notes you have made from Grandfather's notebook. I am glad you have written everything down in your own book as well. Comparing the two copies when we meet will be a good way to make sure nothing has been missed or misread. The entries you sent seem clear enough, though I share your hesitation about the lunar dates. Father has promised to sit with us and go through the whole notebook page by page. He says there are also some loose pages tucked between the covers, which he had forgotten about. I will ask him to bring them out when we meet.

The photograph you sent of the family gathering at your place is lovely. I have put it on the sideboard next to the one of Mother and Father taken at their wedding. The children keep asking who everyone is, and I have been telling them the names. Mei Ling, who is now a big girl of nine, was very taken with the picture of herself as a baby in your arms. She says she does not remember being so small. I told her that none of us remember being so small, but the photograph keeps it true for us. She has started to ask about our grandparents, and I realise I do not know as much as I should. Perhaps when we meet, you can tell me more stories.

The weather here continues to be hot and dry. The well in the backyard has not risen much despite the prayers. Mrs. Pereira's prayer group has grown a little; there are now six of us who meet on Sundays after mass. I find it a comfort, though I cannot say it has changed the weather. Father says the rain will come when it comes, and we must be patient. He spends much of his time now in the garden, trying to keep the plants alive with the little water we can spare. The chillies and the pandan are doing better than the vegetables. He says the soil is too dry for the beans.

I have been thinking about what you wrote concerning the old family stories. You mentioned that Uncle Chye once said our great-grandfather came from a village near the coast. I remember hearing something like that as a child, but I do not recall the details. There is an old letter, I think, from a cousin in China that mentions the village name, but I am not sure where it is kept. Perhaps it is among the loose pages Father has. I will ask him to look for it. The letter, if it can be found, might have more information about the family before our grandfather came to Singapore. I have also heard, from Aunt Lan, that there was once a family register kept by the eldest son of each generation. She says it was lost during the war, when the house was searched. It is a pity, for such a register would be a great treasure now. But we must make do with what remains.

I have written a few notes of my own from memory, as you suggested. They are not as complete as the entries from Grandfather's notebook, but they may help to fill some gaps. I have set them down in the same book I use for household accounts, in the back pages. Here is what I have:

- Our grandmother's name was Lim Ah Choo. She was born, I believe, in 1885, but I am not certain of the month or day. The date was never recorded, as far as I know.
- Our mother, Tan Boon Chye's wife, was named Ng Siew Kim. She was born in 1912, I think, but again I am not sure of the exact day.
- I remember that our grandfather, Tan Ah Kow, had a brother named Tan Ah Kim, who went to live in Penang. I do not know if he had children.
- Uncle Chye has always said that he was born in the year of the Monkey, which matches the notebook. He was born in 1908, as you have written.
- I have a vague memory that our aunt, Tan Chye Neo, was born in the year of the Tiger, but I cannot say which year exactly. Perhaps it was 1914 or 1926? I do not trust my memory on this.

listed in the application file, and the genealogical search report (TEO-GEN-2021). The
following points were discussed:

- The applicant's birth certificate (Reg. No. 1976/12345) and the birth certificate of
  her mother, Tan Poh Choo (Reg. No. 1948/6789), establish the line of descent from
  Tan Ah Seng and Lim Guat Eng to the applicant. The death certificate of Tan Ah Seng
  (Reg. No. 1985/2345) was also verified.

- The applicant's relationship to Tan Kim Huat is through her great-grandfather, Tan
  Ah Seng. The death of Tan Kim Huat in 1942 is documented in family records but the
  original death certificate could not be located due to wartime losses. A statutory
  declaration was submitted by the applicant's mother, Tan Poh Choo, affirming the
  family history. The panel accepted this declaration in accordance with Clause 4.2
  (c) of the Tan Estate Office Rules (rev. 2020).

- No competing claims were identified in the genealogical index search conducted
  23–26 March 2021.

Decision: APPROVED
Conditions: None
Effective Date of Approval: 8 April 2021

The review notes indicate Tan Mei Ling's application_status is approved. Record status: current. The approval
is current and has not been superseded by any subsequent action.

2. Post-Decision Actions

2.1 Notification to Applicant
Date of Notification: 12 April 2021
Method: Registered mail to address on file (Blk 123, Tampines Street 11, #04-56,
Singapore 521123).
Acknowledgement of receipt: Received on 15 April 2021 (signed by applicant).

2.2 File Indexing
The application file was indexed under TEO-EL-2021-0147 in the Tan Estate Office
eligibility register on 13 April 2021. The register entry includes the following:

- Applicant name: Tan Mei Ling
- Relationship: Great-granddaughter of Tan Kim Huat
- Date of approval: 8 April 2021
- Status: Approved (current)

The register was updated to reflect the approval on 13 April 2021. No subsequent
amendments have been made to this entry.

2.3 Supporting Documents Return
The original supporting documents (birth certificates, death certificate, statutory
declaration) were returned to the applicant on 16 April 2021 via registered mail.
Copies of all documents are retained in the application file.

3. Related Applications Reviewed in the Same Period

The following applications were also reviewed by the panel during the April 2021
sitting. These notes are included for completeness of the review record.

3.1 TEER-2021-0152 – Tan Boon Hwa
Relationship Claimed: Grandson of Tan Ah Seng (through son Tan Ah Kow)
Stage 2 Screening Result: PASSED (screened by A. Rahim, 30 March 2021)
Stage 3 Panel Deliberation: 8 April 2021
Decision: REJECTED
Reason: The applicant's birth certificate (Reg. No. 1952/4567) lists father as
Tan Ah Kow, but the birth certificate of Tan Ah Kow (Reg. No. 1920/3456) lists father
as Tan Ah Seng. The panel noted that Tan Ah Kow's birth certificate does not match
the family tree submitted by the applicant. The applicant could not provide a
satisfactory explanation for the discrepancy. Eligibility criteria under Clause 4.2
were not met.
Rejection Notification: Sent on 15 April 2021.
Appeal: No appeal received as of 30 April 2021.
